questions.answer: The identity matrix has 1 on the main diagonal and 0 everywhere else. Therefore \(I_3\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\).
A zero matrix has every entry equal to 0. A \(2\times 4\) matrix has 2 rows and 4 columns. Therefore the \(2\times 4\) zero matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&0\\0&0&0&0\end{pmatrix}\).
Multiplying on the right by the \(2\times 2\) identity matrix leaves a \(2\times 2\) matrix unchanged. Therefore \(AI_2=A\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\), compute 0A where 0 is the \(2\times 2\) zero matrix.
questions.answer: The product of a compatible zero matrix with A is a zero matrix. Here 0 is \(2\times 2\) and A is \(2\times 2\), so 0A is \(2\times 2\). Every row-column product contains only zeros from the left factor, so 0A = \(\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: If A is \(3\times 5\), which identity matrix makes AI valid: \(I_3\), \(I_5\), or both?
questions.answer: For AI to be valid, the identity matrix on the right must have rows equal to the number of columns of A. Since A is \(3\times 5\), it has 5 columns. Therefore AI_5 is valid and equals A. AI_3 is not defined because the inner sizes would be 5 and 3. The correct choice is \(I_5\) only.

questions.prompt: If A is \(3\times 5\), which identity matrix makes IA valid: \(I_3\), \(I_5\), or both?
questions.answer: For IA to be valid, the identity matrix on the left must have columns equal to the number of rows of A. Since A has 3 rows, I_3A is valid and equals A. I_5A is not defined because the inner sizes would be 5 and 3. The correct choice is \(I_3\) only.

The matrix on the left is \(2\times 3\). Multiplying by \(I_3\) on the right is defined and leaves the matrix unchanged because \(I_3\) is the identity for 3-component columns. Therefore \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{pmatrix}\)\(I_3\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: Find x and y if \(\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\0&y\end{pmatrix}\) is the \(2\times 2\) identity matrix.
questions.answer: The \(2\times 2\) identity matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). Match corresponding entries. The top-left entry gives \(x=1\), and the bottom-right entry gives \(y=1\). Therefore \(x=1\) and \(y=1\).

questions.prompt: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}4&5\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\), simplify \(A0\) + BI_2, where 0 is the \(2\times 2\) zero matrix.
questions.answer: First, \(A0\) is the \(2\times 2\) zero matrix because multiplying by a compatible zero matrix gives zero. Second, \(BI_2=B\) because \(I_2\) is the \(2\times 2\) identity matrix. Therefore \(A0\) + \(BI_2=0\) + \(B=B\) = \(\begin{pmatrix}4&5\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: A student says the zero matrix and identity matrix are the same because both are special square matrices. Diagnose the error using \(2\times 2\) examples.
questions.answer: The \(2\times 2\) zero matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\), while the \(2\times 2\) identity matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). They are not equal because their diagonal entries differ. Their roles are also different: adding the zero matrix leaves a matrix unchanged, while multiplying by the identity matrix leaves a compatible matrix unchanged. Therefore they are different special matrices.
